components.text: Contingent beings and their totality require an external sufficient reason.
The explanatory terminus is a being whose nonexistence is impossible.
Individual contingent beings lack the complete reason for their existence.
The totality of those beings therefore requires an external existent reason.
A complete explanation must terminate in a being that cannot fail to exist.
Necessity has significant application only to analytic propositions.
A necessary being requires a self-contradictory denial of existence.
Necessity applies significantly only to analytic propositions.
A necessary being is admissible only when denying its existence is self-contradictory.
A contingent being lacks the complete reason for its existence.
A necessary being must exist and cannot fail to exist.
A contingent being lacks its complete reason and depends on something external.
A necessary being must exist and cannot fail to exist.
The series must be either caused or uncaused.
An uncaused series would be self-sufficient and therefore necessary.
The contingent series consequently must possess an external cause.
The series must consequently possess a cause external to itself.
A series of wholly contingent members cannot itself be necessary.
The series as a whole must fall under a demand for causal explanation.
An uncaused series would therefore be self-sufficient and necessary.
Mystical experience presents itself as awareness of a transcendent object.
A wholly subjective account leaves explanatory residue.
An objective divine cause is the best explanation of the experience.
An objective cause explains the experience better than a wholly subjective account.
The claim is explanatory rather than a strict deductive proof.

Human beings widely experience a distinctive consciousness of moral obligation.
That consciousness is best explained by a transcendent ground of value.
The transcendent ground functions as a non-arbitrary author of moral law.
The authority of moral law points to a non-arbitrary transcendent author.
Objective moral obligation is best explained by a transcendent ground of value.
Widespread human consciousness includes a distinctive sense of moral obligation.
